newsitem.title: USA: Swiss name war victims whose assets went to Poland.
newsitem.headline: Swiss name war victims whose assets went to Poland.

text.p: In a rare break with its traditional bank secrecy, Switzerland on Wednesday gave a Jewish group the names of Holocaust victims whose Swiss bank accounts were given to Poland's Communist government on the grounds that they had died and had no heirs.

The 53 accounts, totalling 464,000 Swiss francs when they were declared dormant and heirless in a 1949 treaty between the two countries, were not turned over to Poland until 1975. Switzerland did not tell Poland to whom the money belonged.

Jewish groups charge that Poland used some of the money to compensate Swiss citizens whose Polish property had been nationalised. The rest was believed to have gone into the country's general treasury.

World Jewish Congress Vice President Kalman Sultanik said he received the list from the Swiss government and was shocked to discover that many of the accounts listed heirs and legal representatives that the Swiss could have contacted had they sought to return the money.

"We are grateful for the list and we are appalled at what it contains. The Swiss claim they turned over heirless accounts of Polish citizens to Poland. Now we see that many of these accounts give the names and addresses of heirs and representatives -- not only in Poland but in places like Rio de Janeiro, London, Paris, Long Island, N.Y., and Amsterdam."

"We also see that the Swiss banks had contacts with some account holders as late as May 1945," and it was difficult to see how they could determine in 1949 that the accounts were dormant and the account-holders dead and heirless, he said.
Switzerland has said it did not give Poland the names for fear the then-Communist government would punish the account holders or their heirs for having foreign bank accounts.

U.S. Senate Banking Committee Alfonse D'Amato late last year made the Polish-Swiss treaty a subject of controversy, charging that the 1949 treaty contained a secret provision under which Poland would receive the dormant, heirless accounts and that it allowed Swiss citizens to be compensated by Poland with money from Holocaust victims.
The Swiss government denied the provision was secret but agreed it had not been publicised. It also said the funds from the heirless accounts did not go directly to Swiss citizens.

Sultanik said about 50 of the 53 accounts appeared to belong to Jews. He said all the information on the accounts, including names and addresses, would be published on Thursday in the Jewish Week newspaper in the hopes of finding heirs or survivors.
The accounts range from 5.5 Swiss francs held by a man in Lemberg to 73,272.8 francs in the account of a man from Danzig.
